study_goal: Understand how energy and matter move through photosynthesis and respiration

prior_sessions.learner_quote: I know the plant needs CO₂, but I keep picturing sunlight going into the glucose as a kind of ingredient.
If something has more energy, does it have more stuff in it? I think that might be how sugar gets bigger.
The carbon atoms in new sugar have to come from something that has carbon atoms.
In mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix into the intermembrane space.
I thought the chloroplast stroma was where the extra protons pile up because the matrix is inside mitochondria.
I know the mitochondria diagram, but the labels on the chloroplast version throw me off.

provisional_root_hypotheses.presenting_difficulty: Does sunlight become part of sugar?
provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May be treating transferred energy as physical matter incorporated into products
alternative_hypotheses: Uncertain about specific atom sources despite knowing energy-matter distinction

provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May overgeneralize the mitochondrial spatial representation to chloroplasts
alternative_hypotheses: Unfamiliar with chloroplast vocabulary rather than transfer failure

learner_specific_relationship_hypotheses.claim: Correctly described proton pumping in mitochondria, but mapped it incorrectly in chloroplasts

study_goal: Explain the role of carbon dioxide and trace atoms through photosynthesis

prior_sessions.learner_quote: Light is energy, not matter. It does not provide carbon atoms.
If I count all the atoms in a closed chemical reaction, I should find the same elements before and after.
Does sunlight become part of sugar? The diagrams never show me which molecule brings the carbon in.
I know CO₂ contains carbon, but I cannot work out where that atom appears in the glucose drawing.
I can tell you Rubisco fixes CO₂, but I lose track of it when the carbon compounds rearrange.
If 8 units go in and 5 leave every minute, I think the pool grows by three each minute.

provisional_root_hypotheses.presenting_difficulty: Does sunlight become part of sugar?
provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May lack an atom-tracking model of carbon fixation and rearrangement
alternative_hypotheses: May be confused about energy and matter

provisional_root_hypotheses.presenting_difficulty: Cannot track carbon atoms through the Calvin cycle
provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May lose track of atom conservation across intermediate rearrangements
alternative_hypotheses: May only be unfamiliar with diagram labels

learner_specific_relationship_hypotheses.claim: States conservation correctly, but does not yet apply it when tracing rearranged carbon compounds

study_goal: Transfer ion-gradient reasoning to neurons, mitochondria and kidney transport

prior_sessions.learner_quote: I think a channel and a pump are almost the same because both let ions go through.
Particles move down their concentration gradient, so protons must be pumped down the gradient by ATP synthase.
Opening sodium channels tends to depolarize the membrane.
I keep mixing up the pump that builds the proton gradient with ATP synthase that uses it.
I thought the sodium-glucose cotransporter makes the Na⁺ gradient itself.
I got the multiple choice right after the hint, but I am not sure I could explain it without the options.

provisional_root_hypotheses.presenting_difficulty: Confuses active proton pumping with downhill H⁺ flow
provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May not distinguish energy-input transport from gradient-driven transport
alternative_hypotheses: May misunderstand electrochemical versus concentration gradients

provisional_root_hypotheses.underlying_cause_hypothesis: May apply the same pump/channel confusion to renal sodium-glucose transport
alternative_hypotheses: May simply not know the kidney-specific transporters

learner_specific_relationship_hypotheses.claim: May conflate gradient-building transport with gradient-using transport in both bioenergetics and kidney physiology
